data.title: Designing for changeover, not just throughput
data.excerpt: A line optimised for one product is a line that punishes every product after it. Changeover is a design constraint, not an operator problem.
data.body:
Throughput is easy to sell. A single number, measured on a good day, with a stable product and a settled crew. Real plants rarely operate under those conditions for long.

Changeover exposes the quality of the whole system: tooling design, recipe management, quality gates, material staging, and the operator's mental model. When those are treated as separate projects, every product change becomes an escalation.

The four seams of a changeover

We look at four seams: the physical change (tooling, fixtures, cleaning), the digital change (recipes, parameters, traceability), the quality change (first-off inspection, approvals), and the human change (who decides, who verifies, what good looks like).

  • Design tooling for repeatable location, not just fit.

  • Make recipes versioned and testable before the line stops.

  • Move first-off inspection into the changeover standard.

  • Measure changeover from last good part to next good part, not from stop to start.

Buy capability, not speed

A line that changes over in twenty minutes but needs an engineer every time is less capable than a slower line the team can run itself. Capability includes recoverability, documentation, and the confidence to try the next product.
